## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and catalog data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Sabhiya Sutta* (Snp 3.6) is a major discourse found in the *Mahāvagga* of the *Suttanipāta* [Norman 1983]. Set early in the Buddha's teaching career, the sutta recounts the visit of the wanderer (*paribbājaka*) Sabhiya, who, unsatisfied by the responses of renowned contemporary teachers, questions the Buddha regarding the characteristics of a true holy man [Norman 1983]. Sabhiya asks for the definitions of traditional religious designations such as *brāhmaṇa*, *samaṇa*, *nhātaka*, and *bhikkhu*; the Buddha responds by redefining and moralizing these terms through didactic folk etymologies (*nirukti*) and verbal wordplay [Norman 1980; Norman 1983; Williams, Origins]. Metrically, the verses (vv. 510–540) are composed principally in the Aupacchandasaka metre, interspersed with Vaitālīya and occasional Śloka pādas [Norman 1997–2001].

The sutta is of central importance for the linguistic and historical study of early Buddhist texts. A parallel Buddhist Hybrid Sanskrit version is preserved in the Lokottaravādin *Mahāvastu*, where the wanderer is named Sabhika [Norman 1980; Norman 1983]. Philological analysis shows that the sutta was composed in an early Middle Indo-Aryan Prakrit featuring the reduction of intervocalic stops to glides (*-k-* and *-c-/-j-* to *-y-*), as shown by the dialectal alternation between *Sabhiya* and *Sabhika*, as well as textual doublets like Pali *virajo* alongside *Mahāvastu* *virato* [Norman 1980; Norman 1997–2001; Levman 2014]. Because cognate recensions exist in both the Theravāda and Mahāsāṅghika-Lokottaravādin traditions, scholars infer that the core text antedates the schism between these schools [Norman 1980]. While G. C. Pande considered the sutta's intricate form and mention of sixty-three śramaṇic views indicative of a later doctrinal layer [Pande 1974], K. R. Norman pointed out that displaced pādas and corruptions in the Pali verse tradition contrast with the commentary, which preserved independent archaic readings [Norman, Philological Approach].

 This relationship is confirmed by DharmaNexus, which computes 99 cross-language alignments with the *Mahāvastu-avadāna*, along with matches in the *Saṅghabhedavastu*, *Divyāvadāna*, *Udānavarga*, and Chinese *Saṃyuktāgama* [DharmaNexus]. Within the Pali canon, DharmaNexus identifies 976 text-reuse passages across 83 texts, notably with the *Brāhmaṇa Saṁyutta* (SN 7), the *Mahākhandhaka* (Kd 1), the *Mahāparinibbāna Sutta* (DN 16), and the *Māgaṇḍiya Sutta* (MN 75) [DharmaNexus]. Canonical exegetical works, including the *Mahāniddesa*, *Cullaniddesa*, and *Nettippakaraṇa*, cite the sutta extensively.
